KEY MESSAGE 1...As of 1:40 PM EDT...High pressure has shifted 
off to the south and east with a warm front located just south 
and west of our region. Current GOES 16 WV imagery shows an 
upper trough dropping down from Canada and another upper 
shortwave back over the Great Lakes. The upper forcing for 
ascent is leading to some scattered showers for northern areas 
based on latest radar imagery, with additional showers and 
perhaps a few thunderstorms expected this afternoon further 
south where low- level positive theta e advection will also lead
to some enhanced lift across the Mid Hudson Valley. While deep-
layer shear is fairly strong, lack of instability (<500 J/kg of
SBCAPE per the latest SPC mesoanalysis), mid-level capping, and
meager mid- level lapse rates will all work to limit the threat
of severe weather. A few non-severe thunderstorms will still be
possible, though, mainly for our southern few counties. We 
collaborated with WPC to have the marginal risk ERO removed 
entirely from our region today given fast storm motions and lack
of instability should prevent any sort of flooding threat. 

Tonight, as the upper trough tracks by to the north it will help 
push a cold front southwards through the region, with a ridge of sfc 
high pressure building down from the north in its wake. This will 
lead to a drying out trend overnight tonight. Some patchy fog or low 
stratus will be possible, especially in the river valleys and for 
anywhere that sees rain this afternoon/evening. It should be another 
comfortable night with lows mainly in the 50s. Tomorrow, the ridge 
of high pressure remains overhead to start the day, but retreats 
to the north as the day progresses. The cold frontal boundary 
will stall to our south and west tonight, but is expected to 
begin to lift back north tomorrow afternoon. The day will start 
off dry area- wide, but a few afternoon showers will be possible
especially for our west/southwestern areas with/ahead of the 
advancing warm front. Not expecting much if any thunder through 
tomorrow afternoon due to lack of instability.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Long term period will feature upper ridging 
over the center of the country, with multiple upper shortwave 
disturbances embedded in W/NW flow around the periphery of the 
upper ridge tracking over the Northeast. Severe weather 
potential will ultimately come down to timing of these 
disturbances in relation to daytime heating and the location of 
a frontal boundary that will be located nearby, which both 
remain somewhat uncertain at this juncture. Generally near
normal temperatures with increasing humidity expected through
most of the week, although temps could reach the mid 80s for
southern areas if the aforementioned frontal boundary is able 
to lift far enough north and east Tuesday.

Monday night into Tuesday morning, guidance has come into decent 
agreement for areas of showers as the warm front lifts
northeastwards and an upper disturbance associated with 
remnant/decaying MCS activity tracks over the region. Showalter 
values become negative Monday night, so some thunder will be 
possible, but not expecting any severe weather at this time with
this instability remaining elevated. WPC has kept most of our 
region in the marginal risk ERO, and some minor hydro issues 
can't be ruled out if we see training of storms, but overall 
hydro threat still appears rather low at this time.

Tuesday...Seeing increasing consensus for remnant shower activity 
and clouds tracking off to our east at some point Tuesday 
morning. Tuesday afternoon is looking potentially active, but a 
few points of uncertainty remain. First, the sfc warm front will
likely be located somewhere near our western CWA border with 
BGM. How far it advances into our region Tuesday afternoon will 
determine which areas may see afternoon strong to severe storms.
At this point, most likely areas seem to be eastern Catskills 
and Mid Hudson Valley, as well as possibly the western Mohawk 
Valley. South and west of the warm front, up to 2000-3000 J/kg 
of SBCAPE is expected to overlap with 35-45 kt of deep-layer 
shear. So the parameter space looks quite favorable for severe 
weather, although it remains to be seen just how far into our 
CWA this favorable environment is able to advance. Other 
question is if morning convection/cloud cover will linger long 
enough limit the recovery and amount of instability around in 
the afternoon, which could also reduce the severe threat. 
Locally heavy rain will be possible with some of these storms as
well as PWATs rise to 1.6-1.9". Timing for any severe storms 
would likely be mid afternoon into the evening with an 
approaching upper disturbance, the warm front, and any remnant 
outflow boundaries from the morning convection acting as foci 
for CI. The overnight SPC day 3 convective outlook just has a 
marginal risk south and west of the Capital District right now, 
but if current trends continue then an upgrade to a slight risk
